newsitem.title: United Nations: Russia opposes expansion of NATO structures.
newsitem.headline: Russia opposes expansion of NATO structures.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Tuesday Moscow opposed the eastward expansion of NATO's military structures but he appeared not to rule out Russia's former allies joining the Western alliance.

"We do not accept either the idea of the expansion of the NATO military infrastructure to the area of the former and now extinct Warsaw Treaty or the efforts to transform this alliance into an axis of a new European system," he told the U.N. General Assembly.

NATO plans to call a summit next spring or summer to name the first former Warsaw Pact countries to be accepted into the alliance, with Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary the most likely candidates. The United States and its allies say they are determined to go ahead with expansion and are seeking to sweeten the pill for Russia by drawing up a special charter on ties with Moscow.
But Primakov said after talks with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Monday that the United States and Russia still had "different approaches" to the issue.

In a text of his U.N. speech distributed in advance, Primakov said Russia "cannot ignore reality" and accepted that NATO would have an important place in European security. But he omitted this remark in his delivered speech.

Earlier, Russian security chief Alexander Lebed was quoted as taking a tough line and saying Moscow would hit back at German and U.S. industrial interests in Russia if the West allowed NATO expansion to the former superpower's borders.

Lebed told London's Daily Telegraph newspaper in an interview published on Tuesday that Moscow felt deeply threatened by the expansion plan and suggested Germany was trying to build a new empire in the East.

Primakov repeated a long-standing Moscow call for an "all-European system of international relations" based on the Organisation for Security and Cooperation and Security in Europe (OSCE), which holds a Lisbon summit in December.

Primakov made clear last week that what he mainly objected to was the stationing of NATO troops and weapons closer to Russia's borders. But Lebed's reported remarks on Tuesday suggested he opposed any kind of NATO expansion.

Primakov also called on Tuesday for an international military and police presence, with Russian participation, to continue in Bosnia even after the NATO-led peace implementation force IFOR ends its mission in the Balkan republic in December.

Western officials increasingly accept that a follow-on force will be needed, although U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Tuesday it was too early to speculate on it. The subject is politically sensitive in the United States ahead of Nov. 5 presidential elections.

Primakov called for the rapid lifting of U.N. sanctions against rump Yugoslavia and the Bosnian Serbs and full re-admission of Yugoslavia to the United Nations after the holding of Bosnian elections 10 days ago.

He pledged continuing efforts to achieve peace in rebel Chechnya, where tens of thousands have died since a Russian military intervention in December 1994, but he made no concession to Chechen separatist aspirations.
"Our goal is to safeguard the legal rights of the Chechen people while unconditionally maintaining Russia's territorial integrity," he said. A new ceasefire in Chechnya was negotiated on Aug. 31.
